Small Silurian-age faults offset the rock layers here, juxtaposing a weaker layer against a stronger cap; the sea has spent thousands of years since exploiting exactly that weakness, hollowing out cave after cave along the fault line while the harder rock above holds firm. One of the larger caves, resembling a vaulted ceiling, has long been nicknamed Cathedral Rock.
properties.source: Maine Geological Survey, Maine Geologic Facts and Localities — The Ovens, Bar Harbor, ME

properties.title: Sand and mud on top of a much older rock
properties.place: Bar Harbor Formation, Mount Desert Island
properties.body: Much of eastern Mount Desert Island's bedrock is the Bar Harbor Formation — sandstone and siltstone hardened from sand and silt that accumulated on top of the much older Ellsworth Schist, itself a metamorphic rock formed long before this later sediment ever settled on it. It's a genuine layered stratigraphic sequence, older rock buried under younger, distinct from the separately-formed volcanic rocks of the nearby Cranberry Isles — a reminder that "Mount Desert Island granite" is really shorthand for at least three or four different rock stories stacked, intruded, and eroded together over hundreds of millions of years.
properties.source: National Park Service Geodiversity Atlas — Acadia National Park, Maine

properties.title: Named for the bog, then set off on its own
properties.body:
The Cranberry Isles take their name from an actual 200-acre wild cranberry marsh on Great Cranberry Island — a name prominent enough by 1762 that it shaped Massachusetts Governor Francis Bernard's land grant for the area that same year (the same Bernard grant that, in a roundabout way, later fed into the Cadillac/Gregoire land dispute over Mount Desert Island itself). The earliest arrivals were transient — fishing, cutting barrel staves, then moving on — but the Bunker, Spurling, and Stanley families became the first to actually stay.

On March 16, 1830, the Maine Legislature set off Great Cranberry, Little Cranberry (Islesford), Sutton's, Baker's, and Bear Islands from the town of Mount Desert, incorporating them as their own town: Cranberry Isles, with Samuel Hadlock, Enoch Spurling, and Joseph Moore as first selectmen. The new town annexed additional Mount Desert land in 1849.
properties.source: Cranberry Isles, Maine — Wikipedia

properties.title: The keeper who wouldn't switch parties
properties.body:
William and Hannah Gilley settled Baker Island around 1806 with two or three young children; by 1826 they had twelve. Two of their sons stayed on with families of their own, growing the island's year-round population to around twenty through the rest of the century. The U.S. Lighthouse Service built a lighthouse and keeper's house here in 1828 for $3,798.26, and William Gilley became its first keeper.

Lighthouse keeperships were political patronage jobs in that era, awarded and revoked with the White House. When Whig candidate Zachary Taylor won the presidency, Gilley — a Democrat — was offered a choice: switch parties, or lose the job. He refused, reportedly saying he wouldn't switch "for all the lighthouses in the United States," and was fired in 1848 at age 63. He simply moved his operation to Great Duck Island, which he'd already bought in 1837 for $300. An 1898 Portland court ruling later upheld the Gilley family's land claim on Baker Island against a government challenge — the family outlasted the politics that had once cost them the lighthouse.
properties.source: New England Historical Society — William Gilley, 1st Keeper, Baker Island Lighthouse; Keepers of Baker Island — History

properties.title: A ships' store that became an island's memory
properties.body:
Around 1850, Edwin Hadlock built a ships' chandlery on Little Cranberry Island to supply the fishing fleet working these waters; it operated as a store until roughly 1875, then became a general market, then apartments by 1912. Physics professor William Otis Sawtelle bought the building and repurposed it as the "Blue Duck Ships' Store," founding the Islesford Historical Society and using the building as its headquarters and museum starting in 1919 — with a dedicated museum building added in 1927.

The National Park Service acquired the whole property in 1948, folding a private collector's personal preservation project into Acadia National Park itself; it was listed on the National Register of Historic Places on September 30, 1980. A 19th-century chandlery, saved by one professor's fascination with local history, is now a federally protected museum.
properties.source: Wikipedia — Islesford Historical Museum and Blue Duck Ships Store

properties.title: From a captain's launch to a working ferry line
properties.body: In the 1930s, Captain Eber Spurling ran mail out to the Cranberry Isles aboard his own launch, the Jerry — one man, one boat, carrying letters and small freight between the mainland and islands that had no other reliable link to it. Today's Beal & Bunker mailboat fleet, running the Double B and the Sea Queen between Northeast Harbor and the Cranberry Isles, descends directly from that same tradition: a private boat operator filling a gap the state ferry system never quite covered for these particular islands, the way it eventually did for places like Swan's Island.
properties.source: Maine Boats Homes & Harbors

properties.title: The site that proved year-round life on the islands
properties.body:
North Haven holds eight sites on the National Register of Historic Places, every one of them a shell midden — but the Turner Farm Site is the most significant of all, showing three distinct occupation phases stretching back thousands of years. The oldest, the Moorehead phase around 5200 BCE, shows fishing supplemented by hunting land mammals. The Susquehanna phase that followed brought bear, moose, and seals taken from nearby rookeries. The latest, the Ceramic phase, shows something more: year-round occupation with a genuinely diverse food base, not just seasonal visits.

That last point matters — Turner Farm is one of the first sites anywhere on the Maine coast to provide clear evidence that people lived here permanently, all year, long before any European saw the Fox Islands. A 1970s Maine State Museum survey went on to identify more than 49 separate archaeological sites across the island, but Turner Farm remains the one that changed how archaeologists understood pre-contact life on this whole stretch of coast.
properties.source: Wikipedia — Archaeological sites in North Haven, Maine

properties.title: Foxes on the shore, then a town named for a Boston lawyer
properties.body:
English captain Martin Pring named these two islands the Fox Islands in 1603, for the silver-gray foxes he saw along the shore — more than a century and a half before anyone from Europe actually settled them. Massachusetts Bay Colony claimed the islands by 1658, but the first permanent English settler, Thaddeus Carver, didn't arrive from Marshfield, Massachusetts until 1766.

The town covering both islands together incorporated on June 25, 1789, taking the name Vinalhaven after John Vinal, a Boston attorney with no documented connection to the islands beyond however he came to be honored in the naming — a common enough pattern in early Maine town-naming, where the name often tracked land agents, investors, or lawyers rather than settlers themselves. That single town would hold both islands together for the next fifty-eight years, until the split that created North Haven.
properties.source: Wikipedia — Vinalhaven, Maine; Maine: An Encyclopedia — Vinalhaven Island

properties.title: A brief name, then the right one
properties.body:
North Fox Island seceded from the town of Vinalhaven and incorporated as its own town on March 1, 1847 — briefly under the name "Fox Isle," before the legislature settled on North Haven just four and a half months later, on July 13 of that same year. No surviving record spells out exactly why the two islands split after fifty-eight years as one town; what's documented is simply that they did, cleanly and quickly, going from one name to a placeholder to the permanent one inside a single year.

Whatever drove the split, it stuck: North Haven and Vinalhaven have remained two separate towns ever since, sharing the same pair of islands and the thorofare between them, but never reuniting.
properties.source: Wikipedia — North Haven, Maine

properties.title: The quarry owner who became governor
properties.body:
Granite quarrying on Vinalhaven began modestly in the 1820s, then took off after the Civil War. Joseph R. Bodwell opened his own Vinalhaven quarries in 1852 and built the operation into the Bodwell Granite Company, one of Maine's largest employers by the 1880s — big enough that Vinalhaven granite was specified by name in major East Coast building contracts, not just supplied generically. Stone cut on this island went into the Washington Monument and the U.S. Capitol Building itself.

Bodwell didn't stay just a quarry owner: he went on to become Governor of Maine, one of relatively few instances of a Maine granite baron parlaying an island quarry fortune directly into the state's highest office. The company he built ran until 1919, closing in the same general wave of collapse — cheaper steel and concrete — that ended Hurricane Island's quarry nearby around the same period.
properties.source: Meander Maine — Vinalhaven's Granite Legacy; Maine History Journal — Bodwell Blue

properties.title: A lost race, a faster boat, and 140 years of grudge matches
properties.body:
Summer resident William Weld lost a sailing race here in 1883, went home to Massachusetts still stewing about it, and had a faster boat built for the following season — then came back and beat everyone. His brother, impressed rather than annoyed, commissioned four exact copies from local North Haven builder James O. Brown. Those four boats started racing each other in 1885, and the first official, organized race of the class ran on August 15, 1887.

That class — the North Haven Dinghy — is still racing today, making it the oldest continuously-raced one-design sailboat fleet in North America, over 140 consecutive years and counting. A grudge over one lost race in 1883 turned into one of American sailing's longest unbroken traditions, still contested on the same water every summer.
properties.source: Maine Boats Homes & Harbors — Historic Class of Racing Dinghies; North Haven Dinghy Foundation — History

properties.title: The first lobstermen's union in the country
properties.body:
In the winter of 2012-2013, Vinalhaven's lobstermen did something no group of American lobstermen had organized before: faced with low boat prices and mounting friction with the Maine Lobstermen's Association's own leadership, they formed a union — the first lobstermen's union in the United States.

It's a distinctly modern chapter in an old story. This is the same island whose granite quarries once employed hundreds under Joseph Bodwell a century earlier; when that industry finally gave way entirely to fishing, the workers who make their living on the water organized themselves the same way industrial workers had, adapting a labor-movement tool built for factories and quarries to a fishery instead.
properties.source: Wikipedia — Vinalhaven, Maine

properties.title: The 'Red Paint People' were never a people at all
properties.body:
For decades, popular accounts described a mysterious, vanished "Red Paint People" who buried their dead with elaborate red-ocher ceremonies along this coast roughly 5,000 to 3,800 years ago, then disappeared without explanation. Real archaeology tells a different story: this was never a distinct people or race at all, but a shared burial practice — ritual use of powdered red ocher — carried out by multiple separate Archaic-period communities living along the central Gulf of Maine coast. Archaeologists now call the broader tradition these cemeteries belong to the Moorehead burial tradition, spanning a longer stretch of time, roughly 8,500 to 3,700 years ago, than the old "Red Paint" story ever accounted for.

The correction matters: there was no single vanished race practicing a mysterious ritual, just ordinary coastal communities — ancestors of the people who'd later be recorded as Wabanaki — burying their dead with a color and a practice that happened to preserve unusually well in the archaeological record.
properties.source: David Sanger, "'Red Paint People' and Other Myths of Maine Archaeology," Maine History 39.3 (2000); EBSCO Research Starters — Red Paint Culture

properties.title: Whose bay this is
properties.body:
Penobscot Bay and the river that feeds it are the traditional territory of the Penobscot Nation, one of five nations that together make up the Wabanaki Confederacy — alongside the Passamaquoddy, Wolastoqiyik (Maliseet), Mi'kmaq, and Abenaki, each with its own distinct homeland, language, and history across what's now Maine and the Canadian Maritimes. "Wabanaki" itself means, roughly, "people of the dawn land" — the easternmost place the sun reaches on this continent.

The Penobscot Nation's seat today is Indian Island, near Old Town, well up the Penobscot River from the bay itself — a reminder that this coastline was always understood as connected to a much larger inland watershed, not a separate place from it. Every named passage, thorofare, and harbor a modern chart shows in this bay sits within territory the Penobscot Nation has continuously occupied and used for thousands of years before any of those English or French names existed.
properties.source: Abbe Museum — About the Wabanaki Nations; Wikipedia — Penobscot

properties.title: Bashaba, and the war that ended a confederacy
properties.body:
When Samuel de Champlain sailed into the Penobscot River in 1604, he recorded meeting Bashaba — not a personal name but a title, roughly "head chief," held by the sachem who had primacy over the whole Penobscot River region and commanded real influence beyond it. For the next decade, Bashaba's confederacy was the dominant Native power on this stretch of coast.

It ended violently. Around 1615, Mi'kmaq and allied raiders — remembered in English colonial records as "Tarratines" — struck Bashaba's main village in a surprise attack, killing him along with his family and his chief warriors. His confederacy collapsed with him. Then, in 1616 to 1619, a devastating epidemic — likely introduced through earlier European contact — swept the coast, killing an enormous share of the surviving population, just a few years before the Plymouth Colony's founding in 1620. The Wabanaki world English colonists encountered in the 1620s was already a shattered remnant of the one Champlain had described barely fifteen years earlier.
properties.source: Wikipedia — The Tarratine Wars; University of New England — Penobscot Chiefs and Governors

properties.title: A French baron, a Penobscot sachem's daughter, and a village of 160
properties.body:
Jean-Vincent d'Abbadie, Baron de St. Castin, was a French nobleman who came to Bagaduce — present-day Castine — as a young officer and never really left. He married Pidianiske, baptized Molly Mathilde, daughter of a Penobscot sachem, and settled into a genuinely mixed community of roughly 160 people living alongside French Fort Pentagouet, neither purely French nor purely Penobscot but both at once.

St. Castin's marriage wasn't a footnote to the fort's history — it was the reason the fort functioned at all in Wabanaki territory, giving French traders and soldiers a real kinship tie into the Penobscot Nation at a moment when English, French, and Wabanaki interests were all competing for the same stretch of coast. His village and the wars that eventually engulfed it — including Dummer's War in the 1720s, which drew the Penobscot in directly as Wabanaki Confederacy members — make Castine one of the few places on this bay where the cross-cultural reality of 17th-century Maine is this concretely documented, not just implied.
properties.source: Wikipedia — Fort Pentagouet; Island Institute — Castine has rich native history, too; Wikipedia — Dummer's War

properties.title: A living nation, not just a history
properties.place: Upper Penobscot Bay, near the river (regional)
properties.body:
The Penobscot Nation's history on this bay didn't end with colonization — it continues today, actively and sometimes contentiously. The Maine Indian Claims Settlement Act, signed October 10, 1980, formally defined the Penobscot Reservation as Indian Island and every island northward up the river from it, part of a broader settlement covering the Penobscot and Passamaquoddy nations' land claims across the state.

That settlement didn't end the legal questions. A 2015 federal court ruling held that the Penobscot Reservation's boundary doesn't extend to the river's waters themselves, even as it affirmed the tribe's sustenance fishing rights there — a real, unresolved tension between where a reservation's legal line sits and where a nation's actual, lived relationship with the water continues. For a bay whose whole character depends on people's relationship with the water, that's not a historical footnote; it's a live legal and cultural question still being worked out today.
properties.source: Maine Public — Judge: Penobscot Reservation Does Not Include River's Waters (2015); Cultural Survival — We Are a Riverine People: Penobscot Nation, Maine

properties.title: Mountains in winter, the sea in summer
properties.body:
Long before any chart marked this bay's islands by name, Wabanaki families moved through it on a seasonal rhythm: inland toward the mountains and river valleys for winter hunting, back down to the coast every summer for fishing, shellfishing, and gathering, following food rather than staying fixed in one place year-round. Recent GIS research modeling ancestral canoe travel times through the wider Wabanaki homeland (mostly focused on river and portage routes rather than open-water bay crossings) confirms just how much river and seasonal water conditions shaped exactly when and how people could move between those inland and coastal sites.

The islands scattered across Penobscot Bay were never remote or empty in that world — they were seasonal destinations, reached deliberately, on a calendar that repeated every year for thousands of years before European contact interrupted it.
properties.source: National Park Service — Wabanaki Life Thousands of Years Ago; University of New Brunswick — A GIS approach to ancestral Wabanaki canoe routes and travel times

properties.title: A 1,500-year-old village plan, still visible in the ground
properties.body:
A four-acre shell midden on Islesboro, excavated by Maine State Museum archaeologists in 1980, turned out to hold something rarer than the shell itself: the outline of an actual planned village. Semi-subterranean pit-houses, each roughly 3 to 4 meters across, sat arranged in two neat rows of three, parallel to the shore — a layout, not a random scatter of camps. A 13-meter excavation trench turned up fire-cracked rock, charcoal, pottery, and stone tools, including clear evidence that tools were being manufactured on site, not just used and discarded.

Radiocarbon and artifact dating puts the village at roughly 1,500 years old, and its house style — that particular pit-house form — had already fallen out of use by the time Europeans arrived, meaning it represents a way of living on this island that had already changed at least once before Champlain ever sailed past it. It's one of the best-preserved sites of its kind anywhere in northeastern North America, and it's been on the National Register of Historic Places since February 22, 1982.
properties.source: Wikipedia — Archeological Site No. 29-64

properties.title: A 1692 raid, and the tradition it didn't manage to end
properties.place: Seven Hundred Acre Island, near Islesboro
properties.body:
Penobscot and Tarratine people had summered on Islesboro and its neighboring islands to hunt and fish for generations before any European settled there, leaving shell middens along the shore as the physical record of it. In August 1692, during King William's War, English Captain Benjamin Church landed first on Seven Hundred Acre Island, then on Islesboro itself, driving off French traders and Native people he found there and confiscating their beaver and moose pelts — the first recorded European contact on the island, and not a friendly one.

What's easy to miss in that raid's aftermath is what it didn't accomplish: Native people kept coming back. From the mainland, they continued returning to Islesboro afterward to pick berries, dig clams, gather sweetgrass for basketry, and split ash for containers — practices that continued, documented, into the 1930s and '40s before finally fading out. A single violent raid in 1692 didn't sever a relationship with this place that had lasted for centuries before it, and clearly outlasted it by a quarter of a millennium.
properties.source: Islesboro Historical Society via Maine Memory Network — Historical Overview

properties.title: One river, two names, and who was winning
properties.body:
The Etchemin people — ancestral to today's Passamaquoddy Tribe — originally called this river Chiboctous, "big bay," a fitting name for its tidal inlets; Jesuit missionary Pierre Biard recorded Etchemins using that name near the river's mouth in 1611. But the name that stuck and is still used today, Majabigwaduce (shortened in everyday use to Bagaduce), isn't Etchemin at all — it's Mi'kmaq, a nation whose homeland lay in what's now Canada's Maritime provinces and northern Maine.

That naming shift reflects a real shift in power, not just linguistic drift: through the 1500s, the Mi'kmaq built a lucrative firearms-for-furs trade with French traders, then leveraged the resulting military advantage to raid south along this coast, controlling the Penobscot Bay region by around 1600. Captain John Smith's own 1614 map even labels Isle au Haut "the Isle of Sorico" — a name reflecting Mi'kmaq dominance of the area at the time he charted it. The Etchemin name for this river didn't vanish entirely; it survives today in the Passamaquoddy word "Keipokotus."
properties.source: Indian Connections — Mi'kmaqs, Etchemins, and the original name of the Bagaduce River in Maine

properties.title: What the mountain and the river are actually saying
properties.body:
Megunticook — the mountain and lake behind Camden Harbor — is usually translated as "great swells of the sea," though at least one alternate reading gives "at a stream below a height" instead; scholars haven't fully settled which is more accurate. Passagassawakeag, the river running through Belfast, is documented as being "of local Native American origin" and is generally believed to mean "a sturgeon's place" or, more evocatively, "a place for spearing sturgeon by torchlight" — a name that describes an actual fishing technique, not just a location.

Neither name has been definitively traced to one specific Wabanaki nation rather than a general regional usage, so it's fairest to describe both as Wabanaki in origin rather than claim more precision than the sources actually support. What's not in doubt is that both names describe this coast the way the people who lived here first actually used it — as water to fish, not just scenery to look at.
properties.source: Wikipedia — Megunticook Lake; Wikipedia — Passagassawakeag River; Fannie Hardy Eckstorm, Indian Place-Names of the Penobscot Valley and the Maine Coast (1941)

properties.title: A stolen island, and the price of ignoring a complaint
properties.body:
Penobscot people — recorded in colonial documents as "Tarratine Penobscots" — had fished, hunted seabirds and seals, and gathered berries on Matinicus and its neighboring islands for generations before Ebenezer Hall settled there around 1750. Hall burned off grass on neighboring Green Island to make hay for his livestock, destroying land the Penobscot still relied on and depended on seasonally — and their complaints about it went nowhere. By summer 1751, Hall and his son had shot and killed two Native visitors to the island, buried them in Hall's own garden, burned their canoe, and kept their guns. Colonial authorities did nothing; at a formal 1752 conference, Penobscot leader Colonel Louis protested directly — "the land is ours" — and was ignored again.

The Penobscot didn't let it rest. On June 10, 1757, they laid siege to Hall's house, killed and scalped him, and took his wife and two daughters captive. It's a brutal story on both ends, but the actual injustice at its center — a stolen resource, a documented complaint, and years of official indifference before anyone acted — is the part worth understanding, not just the violence it eventually produced.
properties.source: Fishermen's Voice — Genghis Khan, Charlemagne, and Ebenezer Hall; Halls of Bristol County — Ebenezer Hall and Matinicus Island

properties.title: The island that gave Samoset his English
properties.place: Monhegan Island (just west of Penobscot Bay proper)
properties.body:
Monhegan's name is an English corruption of the Abenaki word Monchiggon — "out-to-sea island" — the term used by Samoset, the Wabanaki sagamore famous for walking into Plymouth Colony in March 1621 and greeting the stunned Pilgrims in fluent English. Wabanaki people used Monhegan as a summer fishing camp, not a year-round settlement, working the rich offshore grounds around it each season.

Samoset's English had an ugly origin story behind it: in 1605, English captain George Waymouth kidnapped five Wabanaki men — including one named Assacumet — from near Pemaquid and New Harbor, just west of here, and carried them back to London. Those men spent years among the English before eventually returning to New England, part of the same chain of forced contact that put enough English in Wabanaki hands, a generation later, for a Wabanaki man to be the one doing the greeting when the Pilgrims arrived. Monhegan and Pemaquid sit just west of Penobscot Bay itself, on the Muscongus Bay side, but they're close enough to this cruising ground, and central enough to this history, to belong in the same story.
properties.source: Wikipedia — Monhegan, Maine; Maine: An Encyclopedia — George Waymouth; Wikipedia — Assacumet

properties.title: A place of many fish, and the burial ground Harvard took
properties.body:
The Blue Hill area's Wabanaki name was Alamoosook — "place of many fish" — long before English settlers Joseph Wood and John Roundy landed on Mill Island in 1762 to find land Native people had already known and used for thousands of years. In the late 1930s, an excavation near Blue Hill Bay uncovered at least 43 ancestral human remains and hundreds of associated items, buried beneath a shell midden whose calcium content had counteracted Maine's naturally acidic soil and preserved everything far better than it otherwise would have survived.

Harvard University and its Robert S. Peabody Institute held those remains for decades afterward, and Maine tribes spent years fighting for their repatriation — a dispute that dragged on long after the excavation itself, and one that's forced a real reckoning with how American institutions have historically treated Native ancestors as research material rather than people owed return and rest.
properties.source: Maine Memory Network — Blue Hill; The Maine Monitor — Maine tribes spent decades fighting Harvard for ancestral remains

properties.title: 153 sites, and counting, across two small islands
properties.body:
North Haven's Turner Farm gets most of the attention, but Vinalhaven has its own documented pre-contact archaeology, including a site Maine's own Historic Preservation Commission records as the Candage Site. Across the Fox Islands as a whole — North Haven and Vinalhaven together — 153 recorded prehistoric archaeological sites have been identified, a striking density for two islands that, on a modern chart, mostly read as fishing and quarrying towns rather than as one of the more thoroughly documented pre-contact landscapes on this whole bay.

That density is itself the point: 153 sites isn't the record of occasional visits, it's the record of islands worked, camped on, and returned to constantly, for thousands of years, by people whose presence here didn't leave behind buildings or monuments in the way European settlement later would — just middens, tools, and the kind of evidence archaeologists have spent decades carefully mapping back into a coherent, continuous history.
properties.source: Maine Historic Preservation Commission — prehistoric archaeological site index; Wikipedia — Archeological Site No. 29-64

properties.title: The place of the burning fires
properties.body:
"Schoodic" comes from the Passamaquoddy word "Skutec" — "place of the burning fires" — a name describing generations of use, not a single event. Wabanaki families harvested fish, clams, seabirds, and marine mammals around Frenchman Bay for thousands of years; shell-heap sites here date to somewhere between 1,000 and 2,000 years old, and at least 24 separate Indigenous archaeological sites are documented within what's now Acadia National Park's boundaries, Schoodic included.

University of Maine archaeologist David Sanger — the same researcher who untangled the "Red Paint People" myth elsewhere on this coast — led a student excavation at the Schoodic site itself in 1978, part of a long, ongoing effort to properly document Wabanaki heritage in and around this bay rather than let it stay a footnote to the region's more recently arrived summer-colony history.
properties.source: Maine Indian Tribal-State Commission — Archaeology Then and Now: Exploring Wabanaki Heritage in and around Frenchman Bay; National Park Service — Indigenizing Archaeology at Acadia National Park

properties.title: Stonington Harbor — Anchorage & Moorings

anchorage.moorings: Downtown moorings, wharves, and the fuel dock are reserved for the working fishing fleet, not visitors. There is a two-hour limit at the town float for yachts (drop-off only, not overnight).
anchorage.anchoringNotes: Visiting yachts are welcome to anchor as long as it's clear of the channel and other boats. One spot is roughly 100 yards E/NE of red nun '16' (stay north of it, since it marks the Thorofare edge). A second, quieter overnight spot is about 3/4 mile south of the town dock off the entrance to Mill Pond on Crotch Island.
anchorage.holdingGround: Good holding in mud reported off Crotch Island/Mill Pond entrance, roughly 7 ft at low water.
anchorage.protection: Stonington Harbor itself gives good all-around protection; the Mill Pond/Crotch Island spot is more sheltered but current can run in the Thorofare.
anchorage.notes: The inner harbor is a busy working lobster port with strong tidal current through the Thorofare — expect to share space with commercial traffic and be mindful of gear.

properties.source: Cruising Club of America Cruising Guide to Maine, harbor page for Stonington (guides.cruisingclub.org/harbor/stonington/)

properties.title: Old Quarry Ocean Adventures (Webb Cove) — Moorings

anchorage.moorings: Old Quarry Ocean Adventures maintains 14 moorings on Webb Cove plus a deep-water pier and float; rental moorings and dock space are available to visiting boaters, arranged directly with the operator.
anchorage.anchoringNotes: Not documented in available sources — arrange a mooring or dock space with Old Quarry rather than anchoring on your own in the cove.
anchorage.contact: Old Quarry Ocean Adventures, 130 Settlement Road, Stonington, ME; (207) 367-8977

properties.source: Old Quarry Ocean Adventures listing details via LandVest/Christie's property listing and Visit Maine business directory; location per Mapcarta (Webb Cove, Hancock County, ME)

properties.title: Billings Diesel & Marine — Moorings & Dockage
properties.place: Moose Island, Deer Isle Thorofare (half-mile west of Stonington)

anchorage.moorings: Billings Diesel & Marine maintains 11 granite-block moorings for boats up to 50 ft, plus alongside dockage for vessels up to 75 ft. Both moorings and dockage are first-come, first-served (no reservations).
anchorage.anchoringNotes: Not a self-anchor spot — this is a full-service boatyard; visitors take a mooring or dock alongside.
anchorage.contact: VHF Channel 16; phone (207) 367-2328

properties.source: Cruising Club of America Cruising Guide to Maine (Stonington harbor page) and Billings Diesel & Marine business listings (waterwayguide.com, deerisle.com); coordinates per Waterway Guide marina listing

properties.title: McGlathery Island (Merchant Row) — Anchorage

anchorage.moorings: None — this is a conserved, undeveloped island (owned by Friends of Nature, transferred to Maine Coast Heritage Trust in 2021); no moorings maintained.
anchorage.anchoringNotes: Popular free anchorage; anchor in the cove between Round Island and McGlathery Island for good swinging room, or off the main anchorage in about 21 ft. Pull far enough in for island wind protection; watch for rocks at low tide on the McGlathery side. A kellet is recommended if not on all-chain rode to limit swing.
anchorage.holdingGround: Good holding, reported as mud.
anchorage.protection: Open and exposed to NE; better protection is found tucked closer in toward the islands.
anchorage.notes: Island is part of the Maine Island Trail network — day access for hiking the shoreline/beach is welcomed, but it is a conservation property (no camping fires etc. per standard MITA/MCHT rules).

properties.source: Cruising Club of America Cruising Guide to Maine (McGlathery harbor page), Waterway Guide anchorage listing (McGlathery Island, 2-1712), and Maine Coast Heritage Trust preserve page (mcht.org/preserve/merchant-row/)

properties.title: Camp Island (Merchant Row) — Anchorage

anchorage.moorings: None documented — undeveloped island, self-anchor only.
anchorage.anchoringNotes: Ample anchoring room reported by cruisers, with room to swing near the middle of the Merchant Row island cluster.
anchorage.holdingGround: Good holding in mud and rock.
anchorage.protection: Open and exposed to NE winds/wake.

properties.source: Waterway Guide anchorage listing (Camp Island, 2-1708) and general Merchant Row cruiser reports

properties.title: Isle au Haut Thorofare / Town Landing — Anchorage & Guest Moorings
properties.place: Isle au Haut village, Isle au Haut Thorofare

anchorage.moorings: Three guest moorings are maintained in the Thorofare; described as first-come, first-served, marked with orange balls labeled "Rent." Picking up other private moorings is not allowed.
anchorage.anchoringNotes: Anchoring outside the mooring area/channel is recommended for boats without a guest mooring. Enter between Isle au Haut Light and Sawyer Ledge Buoy '1', passing south of Inner Ledge Daybeacon '3'; favor the north side slightly at the anchorage entrance choke. Channel is under 6 ft at low water — best transited on a rising tide.
anchorage.notes: The town wharf/float (6 ft alongside reported) is a working ferry landing — fine for dropping off passengers, but boats may not be left there. Village store has some provisions, gasoline, and marine supplies; water available from a nearby well.

properties.source: Cruising Club of America Cruising Guide to Maine (Isle au Haut harbor page); Town of Isle au Haut coordinates cross-referenced against Isle au Haut Light (44°03'53"N, 68°39'05"W) and Point Lookout (44°05.047'N, 68°37.932'W)

properties.title: Duck Harbor, Isle au Haut — Anchorage (Acadia National Park)

anchorage.moorings: None — no moorings available. Boats anchor on the shore side of the NPS float only.
anchorage.anchoringNotes: Small anchorage, capacity for only about 4-5 boats; arrive early in the day to get a spot. Best holding is found west of the Acadia National Park float on the harbor's south side. A stern anchor is recommended to control swing, especially with other boats present. Entrance is narrow and easy to miss in fog. Tidal range is at least 10 ft, so the harbor looks very different at high vs. low water.
anchorage.holdingGround: Fairly good holding bottom, but described as needing a properly-sized anchor and rode for the conditions.
anchorage.protection: Protected from harsh wind by Eben's Head just outside the entrance, but exposed to west and southwest winds.

properties.source: Cruising Club of America Cruising Guide to Maine (Duck Harbor at Isle au Haut page); coordinates per Waterway Guide (Duck Island Harbor listing)

properties.title: Sylvester Cove / Deer Isle Yacht Club — Guest Moorings
properties.place: Sylvester Cove, south of Dunham Point, Deer Isle

anchorage.moorings: Deer Isle Yacht Club maintains guest moorings, free of charge, on a strict first-come, first-served basis (cannot be reserved); maximum stay is 3 nights. Visiting boaters are asked to try to contact the club's Harbor Chairman ahead of arrival, who helps assign a mooring.
anchorage.anchoringNotes: An anchorage also exists in the cove south of Dunham Point for boats not on a club mooring.
anchorage.holdingGround: Good holding, mud and rock.
anchorage.protection: Open and exposed to the west.
anchorage.fee: No charge for the guest moorings.
anchorage.contact: Deer Isle Yacht Club Harbor Committee: HarborCommittee@DeerIsleYachtClub.com

properties.source: Deer Isle Yacht Club Mooring Rules & Regulations and Guest Mooring pages (deerisleyachtclub.wildapricot.org); depth/holding/protection and coordinates per Waterway Guide anchorage listing (Sylvester Cove, 2-1706)

properties.title: Buck's Harbor — Moorings & Anchorage
properties.place: South Brooksville, head of Eggemoggin Reach

anchorage.moorings: Two facilities maintain the mooring field: Bucks Harbor Yacht Club (founded 1905) offers a limited number of guest moorings, first-come first-served, not reservable, in depths of roughly 17-35 ft (specific guest balls reported rated for boats up to 35-40 ft). Bucks Harbor Marina separately maintains 30+ moorings for boats up to 70 ft, available seasonally or transiently.
anchorage.anchoringNotes: Not specifically documented as prohibited, but the harbor is a well-established, well-used mooring field — visitors are generally directed to pick up a guest mooring rather than anchor.
anchorage.holdingGround: Good holding ground reported generally in the harbor.
anchorage.protection: Well protected overall — cited as one of the best-protected harbors on this stretch of coast, sheltered in part by Harbor Island.
anchorage.fee: Bucks Harbor Marina charges $50/night for a visitor mooring, including dinghy tie-up, showers, restrooms, WiFi, pump-out, water, trash/recycling, and coin laundry access. BHYC guest mooring fee not confirmed in available sources.
anchorage.contact: Bucks Harbor Yacht Club monitors VHF Channel 9 and can be reached at (207) 326-0556 (staffed weekends from mid-June, daily in July/August).

properties.source: Bucks Harbor Yacht Club Visitors page (bucksharboryc.org/visitors), Bucks Harbor Marina Moorings page (bucksharbor.com/moorings), and Cruising Club of America Cruising Guide to Maine (Buck's Harbor page)

properties.title: Camden Outer Harbor — Anchorage & Moorings

anchorage.moorings: Town-maintained rental moorings and dock space through the Camden Harbormaster's office; private outer-harbor moorings also available from Lyman-Morse and P.G. Willey's Wharf. Cost not confirmed — town fee schedule is published as an annual PDF, not itemized on the harbor department page.
anchorage.anchoringNotes: Very limited anchoring room in the harbor itself, most of which is congested with moorings. The outer harbor anchorage lies eastward of a line from Eaton Point to the buoy north of Curtis Island; depths 13-33 ft.
anchorage.holdingGround: Soft bottom, good holding in the outer harbor anchorage area.
anchorage.protection: Outer anchorage is exposed and known to be rolly, especially near the outer ledges.
anchorage.contact: Harbormaster Steve Pixley — VHF 16 (working channel 11), office (207) 236-7969, cell (207) 691-4314.

properties.source: US Harbors Camden Harbor guide and Camden Harbor Department website (camdenmaine.gov) — harbormaster contact, mooring/dock arrangements, and outer-harbor anchoring depths/holding.

properties.title: Rockport Harbor — Anchorage & Moorings

anchorage.moorings: Close to 300 moorings in the harbor (commercial and recreational); the town mooring field is reported full with no transient town moorings. Rockport Marine (in the outer harbor) rents out some of its own moorings by the night; inner-harbor moorings are reserved for commercial lobster boats.
anchorage.anchoringNotes: Room to anchor in the harbor is available, mainly in the outer harbor.
anchorage.protection: Good protection except from the east.
anchorage.contact: Harbormaster's office (207) 236-0676, aleonard@rockportmaine.gov; VHF 16 monitored at the Rockport Public Landing.

properties.source: Cruising Club of America guide (guides.cruisingclub.org/harbor/rockland) covering Rockport, and Town of Rockport Harbor page (rockportmaine.gov/harbor) — mooring field status and harbormaster contact.

properties.title: Rockland Harbor (Breakwater/Jameson Point) — Anchorage & Moorings

anchorage.moorings: City maintains 20 rental moorings, $50/day or $200/week. Public Landing dock space is first-come, first-served at $2.50/ft/night (including appendages), seasonal floats typically in from mid-May to mid-October.
anchorage.anchoringNotes: Ample designated anchoring space shown on the chart. Two general anchorage areas: one tucked behind the breakwater near Jameson Point (best option, protected from easterly chop), and one in the south corner of the harbor (good in settled weather, but can be affected by seas from the northeast).
anchorage.holdingGround: Sticky mud bottom that holds anchor and chain well.
anchorage.protection: Breakwater/Jameson Point area is protected from easterly chop; the southern anchorage is more exposed to northeast winds.
anchorage.contact: Harbormaster Molly Eddy, (207) 594-0312; office monitors VHF 16 and 09 (also reachable on 11).

properties.source: Cruising Club of America guide (guides.cruisingclub.org/harbor/rockland) and Wikipedia/Fishermen's Voice history of Rockland Breakwater — mooring/dock fees, anchorage locations, holding ground, and harbormaster contact.

properties.title: Gilkey Harbor / Dark Harbor (Islesboro) — Anchorage & Moorings

anchorage.moorings: No town rental moorings in Gilkey Harbor itself. Dark Harbor Boat Yard, in Cradle Cove on Seven Hundred Acre Island, offers about 20 guest moorings at $50/day (first-come, not reservable), plus showers, ship's store, fuel dock, and block ice.
anchorage.anchoringNotes: Anchor in Gilkey Harbor (southwestern side of Islesboro, east of Seven Hundred Acre Island) to access Dark Harbor village; plenty of room to anchor around Cradle Cove between Seven Hundred Acre Island and Spruce Island.
anchorage.holdingGround: Good/excellent holding ground; a secure anchorage frequented by many yachts in summer.
anchorage.contact: Dark Harbor Boat Yard (207) 734-2246; monitors VHF working channels per marina listing.

properties.source: Cruising Club of America guide (guides.cruisingclub.org/harbor/islesboro), US Harbors Gilkey Harbor/Islesboro pages, and Dark Harbor Boat Yard website — mooring counts/cost, anchoring area, and holding ground.

properties.title: Warren Island State Park — Anchorage & Moorings
properties.place: Warren Island State Park, Islesboro, ME

anchorage.moorings: State park mooring field, first-come first-served; reported around 9 moorings (some sources say up to 10) at roughly $20/night, payable ashore. Inner moorings are lighter (150 lb mushroom); the two outermost are 1-ton blocks.
anchorage.anchoringNotes: Water-access-only state park just off Islesboro's Gilkey Harbor approach, about 3 miles offshore from Lincolnville; dinghy dock provided for landing.
anchorage.fee: Approximately $20/night per mooring, paid ashore at the park.

properties.source: Maine Bureau of Parks and Lands Warren Island State Park materials and Waterway Guide anchorage listing — mooring count, type, and nightly fee.

properties.title: Belfast Harbor — Anchorage & Moorings

anchorage.moorings: City-run rental moorings and transient slips available through the Belfast Public Landing/Harbor Office; reservations taken by phone or email ahead of arrival.
anchorage.anchoringNotes: Anchoring permitted only in areas and for durations designated by the harbormaster (per city ordinance); anchor out beyond the mooring field. No boats permitted on the Public Landing docks or rental moorings when SE/ESE winds are forecast over 25 knots.
anchorage.holdingGround: Mud bottom, generally good holding.
anchorage.protection: Exposed to southeasterly winds; channel-traffic wakes can cause rolling as boats swing with tide/current.
anchorage.contact: Harbormaster Kathy Given, (207) 338-1142, harbormaster@cityofbelfast.org; VHF 16, working channel 09.

properties.source: City of Belfast Harbor Department pages (cityofbelfast.org) and Cruising Club of America Belfast guide — mooring/anchoring rules, holding ground, wind exposure, and harbormaster contact.

properties.title: Castine Town Dock — Moorings (Anchoring Not Recommended)

anchorage.moorings: Two visitor moorings reserved primarily for visiting schooners, use requires harbormaster approval. Town Dock floats (seasonal, mid-May to mid-October) offer first-come tie-up limited to 2 hours 9am-5pm, overnight dockage permitted after 5pm at $3/ft/night (up to 80 ft total length).
anchorage.anchoringNotes: Anchoring off the town of Castine itself is not recommended due to poor holding ground and strong currents; cruisers are directed instead to Smith Cove or Holbrook Island area.
anchorage.holdingGround: Poor holding ground in the channel southeast of town (general depth ~72 ft).
anchorage.contact: Harbormaster Scott Vogel, cell (207) 266-9392, dock line (207) 266-7711, on duty 8am-5pm July 1-Labor Day; monitors VHF 09 and 16. Eaton's Boatyard (fuel dock) also on VHF 09.

properties.source: Castine, Maine official 'Arriving by Boat' page (castine.me.us) and Cruising Club of America Castine guide — dockage fees/hours, mooring policy, and note on poor holding off town.

properties.title: Smith Cove (Bagaduce River, near Castine) — Anchorage

anchorage.moorings: No town or commercial mooring field documented; this is an anchor-out cove.
anchorage.anchoringNotes: Popular, spacious anchorage used specifically to avoid the strong currents at the mouth of the Bagaduce River; a preferred alternative to anchoring off Castine itself. Depths run roughly 17-58 ft.
anchorage.holdingGround: Great holding, soft bottom.
anchorage.protection: Excellent protection in all winds; locally regarded as a good hurricane hole.

properties.source: Cruising Club of America guide (guides.cruisingclub.org/harbor/smith-cove) — anchorage character, depths, holding, and all-wind protection; general Castine-area location corroborated by Cape Rosier/Holbrook Island geography.

properties.title: Hurricane Island — Anchorage & Moorings

anchorage.moorings: 6 moorings rated 3,000 lb plus 1 rated 5,000 lb, maintained by the Hurricane Island Foundation (Center for Science and Leadership) on the east side of the island near the main pier; 1-1/8" bottom chain, 1" nylon top gear, inspected annually. First-come, first-served; call ahead on VHF 16 to reserve, as they fill for events/weekends.
anchorage.anchoringNotes: Anchoring in the mooring field is not recommended — the bottom there is littered with debris/artifacts left from the island's granite-quarrying era. A 3.2-acre aquaculture/marine research site off the north end of the island must also be avoided.
anchorage.fee: $25 per night or $15 per day (per Hurricane Island's own facilities page).
anchorage.contact: VHF 16; dockhouse at the head of the main pier; phone (207) 867-6050; email info@hurricaneisland.net.
anchorage.notes: Best approach is from the northeast; an unmarked ledge runs between the mooring field and the rest of Hurricane Sound to the south/southeast.

properties.source: Hurricane Island Center for Science and Leadership facilities page (hurricaneisland.net/facilities) and CCA Cruising Guide to Maine (guides.cruisingclub.org/harbor/hurricane-island/)

properties.title: Carvers Harbor — Anchorage & Moorings

anchorage.moorings: Roughly 100 moorings in the harbor. The town does not rent moorings, but a few private owners leave their moorings open with a "money jar" (average about $30/night, pay on the honor system).
anchorage.anchoringNotes: Not a common anchoring destination — the harbor is dense with private/fishing moorings; visiting boats typically pick up an available private mooring rather than anchor.
anchorage.contact: Harbormaster Jim Knowlton, (207) 756-0209 — can also try to arrange a commercial dock space; dinghy tie-up limited to 16 ft or less at the town dock.
anchorage.notes: Hopkins Boatyard can arrange a transient slip with advance notice and has in-water repair capability; the Fishermen's Co-op doesn't officially take transients but may have room.

properties.source: Maine Boats, Homes & Harbors ("Carvers Harbor," maineboats.com/print/issue-160/carvers-harbor) and Atlantic Cruising Club (atlanticcruisingclub.com/Marinas/2651)

properties.title: Perry Creek — Anchorage & Moorings

anchorage.moorings: A mooring field now dominates what was an undeveloped anchorage; 4 moorings are kept free and are first-come, first-served, with a suggested donation to the Vinalhaven Land Trust, which owns the surrounding land.
anchorage.anchoringNotes: Limited room to anchor in mud with good holding, but moorings occupy most of the usable space. Power cables shown on the chart are real — do not anchor over them.
anchorage.holdingGround: Mud, good holding, where anchoring room exists.
anchorage.protection: All-around protection.
anchorage.notes: Entered from the Fox Islands Thorofare via Seal Cove, curving around Mouse Island. Vinalhaven Land Trust maintains hiking trails from the creek; cell coverage is thin (at most one bar of Verizon).

properties.source: CCA Cruising Guide to Maine, Perry Creek (guides.cruisingclub.org/harbor/perry-creek/); coordinates per USGS topo data via Topozone

properties.title: Seal Bay — Anchorage

anchorage.moorings: No mooring field documented — this is a natural anchorage, not a maintained mooring area.
anchorage.anchoringNotes: Anchoring is the norm here; many possible spots among the bay's coves and islands. The area between Burnt and Hay Islands is a popular hurricane-hole-style anchorage sheltered from big winds. Numerous charted rocks/ledges and lobster gear to navigate around.
anchorage.holdingGround: Good thick mud bottom in the inner harbor areas (per the same source describing the connected Winter Harbor anchoring grounds).
anchorage.protection: All-around protection in the inner coves; the area is comfortable in most conditions but exposed if wind pipes up hard from the north.
anchorage.notes: Entrance is on Vinalhaven's east side, about 1.5-2 miles south of the Fox Islands Thorofare. Bay is largely shallow with ledge/mudflats uncovering at low tide; a dinghy trip at high tide can reach Winter Harbor.

properties.source: CCA Cruising Guide to Maine, Seal Bay plus Winter Harbor (guides.cruisingclub.org/harbor/seal-bay-vinalhaven/); coordinates approximate, derived from chart geography (Burnt/Hay Islands) described in that source

properties.title: Winter Harbor (Vinalhaven) — Anchorage

anchorage.moorings: No maintained mooring field documented.
anchorage.anchoringNotes: Anchor in the deep water between Davids Island (to starboard) and Hay Island (to port) past the unnamed boulders, or continue into the inner harbor past Burnt Island — both areas have good thick mud bottom.
anchorage.holdingGround: Good, thick mud.
anchorage.notes: Reached from Seal Bay; connects to the Mill River and, on the top half of the tide, to a haulover bridge accessible by dinghy. Watch for rocks in the outer entrance and along the Penobscot Island side of the channel. Vinalhaven Land Trust preserves (Lower Mill Preserve, Carrying Place Bridge Preserve) are accessible by dinghy at mid-tide or higher.

properties.source: CCA Cruising Guide to Maine, Seal Bay plus Winter Harbor (guides.cruisingclub.org/harbor/seal-bay-vinalhaven/); coordinates approximate, derived from chart geography described in that source

properties.title: Pulpit Harbor — Anchorage & Moorings

anchorage.moorings: Almost all moorings in the harbor are private — do not pick one up without owner permission. Thayer's Y-Knot Boatyard (Southern Harbor) has installed one rental mooring, about 3-4 boats in from the outer edge of the field; call ahead, (207) 867-4701.
anchorage.anchoringNotes: Anchor in midchannel in the broad part of the harbor, 18-33 ft; a good all-weather spot for small craft is in the southwesterly prong just inside the entrance, 18-27 ft. A more sheltered spot in 8-10 ft is toward the northeast end near the public float. Avoid the crowded, shallow inner harbor.
anchorage.holdingGround: Good holding, mud bottom, in 10-20 ft.
anchorage.protection: Considered a safe, all-weather anchorage.
anchorage.fee: No fee for anchoring; no services of any kind available in the harbor itself (no overboard discharge permitted, no garbage disposal).
anchorage.contact: North Haven Harbormaster (Pulpit Harbor) Adam Campbell, (207) 701-9994, or (207) 867-4433; public landing dinghy dock is the last float before the road bridge.

properties.source: CCA Cruising Guide to Maine, Pulpit Harbor (guides.cruisingclub.org/harbor/pulpit-harbor/) and Town of North Haven, "Sailing to North Haven" (northhavenmaine.org/sailing_to_north_haven.php / departments/harbormaster.php)

properties.title: Southern Harbor — Anchorage & Moorings

anchorage.moorings: Thayer's Y-Knot Boatyard, a full-service yard on site, can provide a limited number of guest moorings (call ahead); they also service moorings out in the Fox Islands Thorofare and Pulpit Harbor.
anchorage.anchoringNotes: A quieter, less-trafficked alternative to Carvers Harbor with room to anchor near the boatyard.
anchorage.contact: Thayer's Y-Knot Boatyard, (207) 867-4701.
anchorage.notes: Approach past Browns Head Light and the Sugarloaves ledges, leaving the Fox's Ear spindle to port, then head due north to the center of outer Southern Harbor toward the boatyard.

properties.source: CCA Cruising Guide to Maine / Town of North Haven "Sailing to North Haven" summary (northhavenmaine.org/sailing_to_north_haven.php); coordinates per Waterway Guide anchorage listing (waterwayguide.com/anchorage/2-1688/southern-harbor)

properties.title: Fox Islands Thorofare (North Haven) — Anchorage & Moorings
properties.place: North Haven village, Fox Islands Thorofare, ME

anchorage.moorings: J.O. Brown & Son / Brown's Boatyard maintains rental moorings suitable for boats up to 60 ft, inspected annually, first-come first-served, plus fuel dock, showers, small chandlery and a haul-out lift.
anchorage.anchoringNotes: Good anchorage can be found in the channel of the Thorofare between the entrance of Seal Cove and the western end of North Haven village.
anchorage.holdingGround: Soft bottom, in depths of 23-33 ft in the main anchoring stretch.
anchorage.fee: $35 per night for a rental mooring at Brown's Boatyard.
anchorage.contact: Thorofare Harbormaster Foy W. Brown, (207) 867-4621 or (207) 867-4433; town dock is just west of the ferry terminal, about 12 ft depth.
anchorage.notes: North Haven is a longstanding summer yacht center; Southern Harbor (west of town) and Waterman Cove (east of town) are cited as additional protected anchorages nearby.

properties.source: Town of North Haven, "Sailing to North Haven" (northhavenmaine.org/sailing_to_north_haven.php) and Town of North Haven Harbormaster page (northhavenmaine.org/departments/harbormaster.php)

properties.title: Valley Cove (Somes Sound) — Anchorage & Moorings
properties.place: Valley Cove, Somes Sound, Mount Desert Island, ME

anchorage.anchoringNotes: Enter Somes Sound through The Narrows; just beyond Sand Point (to starboard), turn to port into Valley Cove and anchor in about 30 feet MLW along the south side of the cove.
anchorage.holdingGround: Bottom is rocky/pebbly in places, but anchors typically find sticky Maine mud that holds well.
anchorage.protection: Excellent protection from prevailing winds inside the cove, though shifting gusts can funnel down off the surrounding mountains (the cliffs of St. Sauveur/Acadia Mountain rise directly from the water here).
anchorage.notes: One of Somes Sound's most popular anchorages — dramatic cliff scenery, close to Fernald Point at the Sound's mouth (site of a short-lived 1613 French Jesuit settlement).

properties.source: CCA Cruising Guide to Maine, Somes Sound entry (https://guides.cruisingclub.org/harbor/somes-sound/). Coordinates (N44°18.538' W068°18.942') from a Waterway Guide anchorage listing (https://www.waterwayguide.com/anchorage/2-2724/valley-cove); direct fetch of that page was blocked (403), so treat the position as approximate, aggregator-sourced.

properties.title: Somes Harbor (Somesville) — Head of Somes Sound Anchorage
properties.place: Somes Harbor, Somesville, Mount Desert Island, ME (head of Somes Sound)

anchorage.moorings: All moorings in Somes Harbor itself are privately owned — best avoided unless you know the owner. Rental moorings are available a short distance south: at Henry R. Abel & Co. Yacht Yard (bookable via Dockwa, (207) 276-5057) and, July–August only, at John M. Williams & Co. Boatyard at Hall Quarry ((207) 244-7854).
anchorage.anchoringNotes: CCA Cruising Guide to Maine describes 'a fine anchorage between Sheep Island and the mainland in about 15 feet MLW' at the head of the sound off Somesville. Entrance is very narrow: leave the red nun marking Myrtle Ledge to starboard, pass the green can close aboard to port, then proceed up to Sheep Island (approx. 44.3642°N, 68.3245°W). Favor the center-to-west side of the sound once past the entrance flasher — the east side shoals. An alternate, more open anchorage in good-holding mud lies about 0.8 nm south, off Abel's Yacht Yard.
anchorage.holdingGround: Not detailed for the Somes Harbor anchorage itself in the CCA guide. The nearby Abel's anchorage (0.8 nm south) is reported as good-holding mud; Valley Cove (2.5 nm south) is rocky/pebbly with pockets of sticky mud.
anchorage.protection: Quiet, well-protected, and serene — described by CCA as a favorite harbor of refuge in nor'easters, tropical storms, and hurricanes. Expect gusty downdrafts off the surrounding mountains.
anchorage.contact: Henry R. Abel & Co. Yacht Yard: (207) 276-5057 (rental moorings via Dockwa). John M. Williams & Co. Boatyard, Hall Quarry: (207) 244-7854 (rental moorings, July–Aug).
anchorage.notes: Somesville town landing floats (NW side) are privately owned but visiting boaters may leave dinghies at the SW corner of the large float (donation requested via QR code). No NPS restriction applies to anchoring in the open water of Somes Sound itself, but two real, park-specific rules apply nearby: (1) Bar Island, near the sound's mouth, is closed to public landing Feb 15–Aug 31 for bald eagle nesting; (2) Acadia-wide, anchoring or tying a boat to shore is prohibited unless attended. The Valley Cove Trail (a popular hike from the Sound's other main anchorage, ~2.5 nm south) is closed Mar 1–Aug 15 for peregrine falcon nesting.

properties.source: CCA Cruising Guide to Maine, Somes Sound entry, read in full (https://guides.cruisingclub.org/harbor/somes-sound/); Acadia National Park Superintendent's Compendium (https://www.nps.gov/acad/learn/management/sc.htm); Sheep Island coordinates from USGS Geographic Names Information System via The History Trust (GNIS Feature ID 575351).

properties.title: Northeast Harbor — Anchorage & Moorings
properties.place: Northeast Harbor, Mount Desert Island, ME

anchorage.moorings: The harbor itself is fully occupied by private and rental moorings, managed by the town-run Northeast Harbor Marina and by Clifton Dock (an arm of the Northeast Harbor Fleet yacht club). Northeast Harbor Marina also has rental slips, bookable via Dockwa.
anchorage.anchoringNotes: There is no room to anchor inside the harbor itself. Good holding and ample swinging room, even for large boats, is available just outside/east of the harbor entrance.
anchorage.protection: The outer anchorage east of the harbor is fine in settled summer weather, but is open to the southwest and east, so it can become breezy and choppy in an afternoon sea breeze.
anchorage.contact: Northeast Harbor Fleet / Clifton Dock: (207) 276-5101, nehfleet@gmail.com, 48 South Shore Road, Northeast Harbor, ME 04662.
anchorage.notes: One of the premier Down East cruising destinations, with full services, restaurants, and provisioning within walking distance of the town dock.

properties.source: CCA Cruising Guide to Maine, Northeast Harbor entry (https://guides.cruisingclub.org/harbor/northeast-harbor/); Northeast Harbor Fleet website (https://www.nehfleet.org/moorings). Coordinates are an approximate position for the harbor entrance/mooring field, not from a specific charted anchorage point.

properties.title: Southwest Harbor — Anchorage & Moorings
properties.place: Southwest Harbor, Mount Desert Island, ME

anchorage.moorings: The Town of Southwest Harbor rents 6 town moorings off the Manset Town Dock (numbered 1–6, yellow-top/white-middle/red-bottom), first-come first-served. Ellis Boat Co. also has 4 rental moorings in the harbor, first-come first-served. Reserve/renew town moorings online at my.onlinemooring.com/southwestharborME/.
anchorage.anchoringNotes: Anchoring inside Southwest Harbor proper is not permitted. Deep-draft vessels can anchor midway between Greening Island and the southern shore in 34–50 ft; smaller vessels can work farther into the harbor in gradually shallower water down to about 12 ft, outside the mooring field.
anchorage.fee: Town (Manset) moorings: $50/night (2025 rate). Ellis Boat Co. moorings: $60/night or $350/week (2025 rate).
anchorage.contact: Harbormaster Rob Leavitt, (207) 610-2177, weekdays 8:30am–5pm. Southwest Harbor Town Office: (207) 244-5404, PO Box 745, Southwest Harbor, ME 04679.
anchorage.notes: Full-service harbor with fuel, provisioning, and marine services; a major hub for MDI's 'quiet side.'

properties.source: Town of Southwest Harbor website (http://www.southwestharbormaine.org/harbor.html); CCA Cruising Guide to Maine, Southwest Harbor entry (https://guides.cruisingclub.org/harbor/southwest-harbor/); Marinas.com Southwest Harbor Town Moorings Anchorage listing. Coordinates are an approximate position for the main harbor/anchoring area.

properties.title: Bass Harbor & Bernard — Anchorage & Moorings

anchorage.moorings: Harbor is dense with private moorings, which can make navigation tight for first-time visitors.
anchorage.anchoringNotes: Best entered at half-tide or better; the channel at the north end passes mud flats that look daunting on a first visit but is straightforward once known.
anchorage.protection: Open only to the south; islands lying off the harbor mouth help shelter it from that direction.
anchorage.fee: Town of Tremont transient dockage (160 ft of float space beside Thurston's Lobster Pound in Bernard): $2.50/ft overnight (recent published rate).
anchorage.contact: Harbormaster Tyler Damon, (207) 244-4564 — call ahead; he will meet visiting yachts near the ferry terminal and guide them in through the mooring field.
anchorage.notes: Gas and diesel available at Thurston's Lobster Pound dock, plus a public boat ramp. Up Harbor Marine (26 Columbia Ave, Bernard, ME 04612) also offers dockage and seasonal waterfront lodging in a protected cove; contact directly for current rates, as none were published on their site. Bass Harbor Bar, just south of the harbor mouth, is a known shoaling area — check current chart/tide before crossing, especially for deeper-draft boats.

properties.source: Waterway Guide Bass Harbor page (https://www.waterwayguide.com/waterway/162/bass-harbor-me — found via search; direct fetch returned 403); Maine Boats, Homes & Harbors, 'Bass Harbor' (https://maineboats.com/print/issue-191/bass-harbor); Up Harbor Marine website (https://www.upharbor.me/). Coordinates are an approximate position centered near Thurston's Lobster Pound dock in Bernard, not from a specific charted point.

properties.title: Bar Harbor — Anchorage & Moorings

anchorage.moorings: Town-managed mooring field in the main harbor near the Municipal Pier (pier listing shows 13 moorings, 4 slips, ~500 ft of dock); a limited number of guest moorings are available nightly. Reserve a town mooring or dock space via Dockwa.
anchorage.anchoringNotes: The anchorage and town moorings lie south of the fairway leading to the town landing and marina. Recommended entry is around Bald Porcupine Island into the harbor; the western entrance inside the breakwater is awash at high tide.
anchorage.protection: Harbor is enclosed by a granite breakwater on its seaward side; open toward the Porcupine Islands in Frenchman Bay.
anchorage.fee: 2025 rates (subject to change): town mooring approx. $57/night; dockage approx. $5.20/ft; an online convenience fee is added to Dockwa bookings.
anchorage.contact: Bar Harbor Harbormaster's Office, (207) 288-5571, VHF 9/16/68.
anchorage.notes: Large dinghy dock and trash dumpster at the town landing, on the west side of the pier, behind the commercial fishing unloading dock.

properties.source: CCA Cruising Guide to Maine (guides.cruisingclub.org/harbor/bar-harbor/); US Harbors Bar Harbor guide (usharbors.com); Bar Harbor Municipal Pier listing on Marinas.com (pier coordinates 44°23'30.47"N 68°12'15.18"W); Bar Harbor Story newsletter, Feb 2025 (mooring/dockage rates, barharborstory.substack.com).

properties.title: Seal Harbor — Anchorage & Moorings

anchorage.moorings: Moorings are administered by the Seal Harbor Town Wharf. Seal Harbor Yacht Club may have slips available to members of reciprocating yacht clubs (call ahead); neither of the harbor's two marina facilities offers dock tie-ups to transients.
anchorage.anchoringNotes: Approach from the south via Eastern Way, where it meets Frenchman Bay. Expect 11-14 ft depths over a sand/rock bottom inside the harbor. Use NOAA Chart 13313.
anchorage.holdingGround: Sand/rock bottom, 11-14 ft depths.
anchorage.notes: No facilities ashore for boaters — come prepared with your own supplies before anchoring or picking up a mooring here.

properties.source: Waterway Guide (waterwayguide.com/directory/anchorage-free-dock/maine/seal-harbor); Marinas.com Seal Harbor listing (coordinates, depth/bottom detail); cross-checked against Wikipedia's Seal Harbor Congregational Church coordinates (44.29361°N, 68.24833°W) to confirm village location.

properties.title: Great Cranberry Island — Anchorage & Moorings
properties.place: Great Cranberry Island, Cranberry Isles, ME

anchorage.moorings: The Town of Cranberry Isles maintains 3 free guest moorings at Great Cranberry, first-come-first-served, usable up to 3 days. They are large white balls with a blue horizontal stripe and 'Town Guest' painted on them.
anchorage.anchoringNotes: Comfortable anchoring with good holding and ample swinging room is available outside the mooring field.
anchorage.holdingGround: Described as good holding outside the mooring field; specific bottom composition not stated in source.
anchorage.fee: Town guest moorings are free (limit 3 days).
anchorage.contact: Cranberry Isles Harbormaster Norman Sanborn Jr., (207) 244-3624 (usually based on Great Cranberry); Deputy Harbormaster Bruce Fernald, (207) 244-5283.
anchorage.notes: Great Cranberry has a well-regarded town dock outside the mooring field with plenty of dinghy space (nicer than Islesford's). Many islanders also keep private boats at nearby Spurling Cove.

properties.source: Waterway Guide anchorage listing (waterwayguide.com/anchorage/2-4394/great-cranberry-island-moorings, page content only partially retrievable) plus general Cranberry Isles cruising-guide coverage (CCA Cruising Guide to Maine, guides.cruisingclub.org/harbor/cranberry-islands/); Wikipedia (Great Cranberry Island — Spurling Cove reference). COORDINATES ARE ESTIMATED: placed near the island's north-end village/town-dock area (opposite Islesford across the harbor) from described geography — no authoritative source for the exact dock position could be retrieved this session.

properties.title: Islesford (Little Cranberry Island) — Anchorage & Moorings
properties.place: Islesford, Little Cranberry Island, Cranberry Isles, ME

anchorage.moorings: The Town of Cranberry Isles maintains 3 free guest moorings at Little Cranberry, first-come-first-served, usable up to 3 days, marked with large white balls with a blue horizontal stripe and 'Town Guest' painted on them. The Islesford Dock Restaurant separately administers transient moorings in Cranberry Harbor and sells gas and diesel.
anchorage.anchoringNotes: Anchoring is not favorable at Little Cranberry — a kelp-covered bottom makes it hard to get a good set.
anchorage.holdingGround: Poor — kelp bottom, difficult to set an anchor.
anchorage.fee: Town guest moorings are free (limit 3 days).
anchorage.contact: Cranberry Isles Harbormaster Norman Sanborn Jr., (207) 244-3624 (usually based on Great Cranberry); Bruce Fernald, (207) 244-5283, available on Little Cranberry as needed.
anchorage.notes: No services on Islesford beyond the Islesford Dock Restaurant; the town dinghy dock is small and often crowded.

properties.source: Cranberry Isles cruising-guide coverage (CCA Cruising Guide to Maine, guides.cruisingclub.org/harbor/cranberry-islands/) and Waterway Guide Cranberry Isles listings. Coordinates taken from Wikipedia's entry for the Islesford Historical Museum and Blue Duck Ships Store (44°15'42"N 68°14'25"W), which sits immediately beside the Islesford town dock — used as a close proxy for harbor position, not the dock itself.

properties.title: WoodenBoat School Waterfront — Anchorage & Moorings
properties.place: WoodenBoat School, Great Cove, Brooklin, ME

anchorage.moorings: WoodenBoat School's own waterfront (Great Cove, at the south end of Eggemoggin Reach) has a float, launching ramp, and 'limited moorings' for visiting boats. If prior arrangements are made, waterfront staff will have a mooring reserved for you; otherwise moorings are used first-come, first-served — the School does not monitor a channel or phone line to report open moorings in real time. Waterfront staff are on duty Mon–Fri 8am until dusk and Sat 1–5pm.
anchorage.anchoringNotes: The School's own materials describe it simply as 'a good anchorage.' It sits on Great Cove on the mainland, across from Babson and Little Babson Islands; Center Harbor and Brooklin Boat Yard are just to the west.
anchorage.protection: Sheltered water at the south end of Eggemoggin Reach, screened by Babson and Little Babson Islands.
anchorage.contact: WoodenBoat School office: (207) 359-4651, school@woodenboat.com. Monitors VHF 16 and/or 68.
anchorage.notes: Dinghy float and showers available for students/guests and their families; no dump/pump-out station at the waterfront. Recognizable from the water by the large white WoodenBoat Publications office building on the hill and a long dock on granite piers. Students/visitors are explicitly welcome to bring their own boat, wooden or not.

properties.source: WoodenBoat School, 'Good Things to Know 2024' (thewoodenboatschool.com/wp-content/uploads/2023/11/Good-Things-to-Know-2024.pdf) — coordinates as stated by the School itself (44°14'45"N, 68°33'25"W).

properties.title: Center Harbor — Anchorage & Moorings

anchorage.moorings: Brooklin Boat Yard rents moorings to visitors — call (207) 359-2236 or hail VHF 18; renters get free showers and laundry at the yard's dockhouse (confirm current nightly rate directly with the yard). Center Harbor Yacht Club does not advertise transient slips but may accommodate members of reciprocal yacht clubs.
anchorage.anchoringNotes: The harbor is 'so choked with moored boats that anchoring safely inside is nearly impossible' — visitors are advised to anchor outboard of the yacht club mooring fleet or rent a mooring from Brooklin Boat Yard. Where there is anchoring room, bottom is soft mud, south of a line between the yacht yard and the entrance daybeacon. Approach from the north via Eggemoggin Reach; the southern approach past Torrey Island is shoal and inadvisable for strangers.
anchorage.holdingGround: Soft mud in the outer-harbor anchoring area.
anchorage.protection: Well sheltered behind Chatto Island, off Eggemoggin Reach.
anchorage.contact: Brooklin Boat Yard: (207) 359-2236, VHF 18, brooklinboatyard.com.
anchorage.notes: Center Harbor Yacht Club pier/float landing (6 ft alongside) is on the north side of the entrance; water available. Center Harbor is known for its fleet of classic wooden yachts, most maintained by Brooklin Boat Yard.

properties.source: Cruising Club of America Digital Cruising Guide to Maine, Eggemoggin Reach entry (guides.cruisingclub.org/harbor/eggemoggin-reach/), read in full; Brooklin Boat Yard (brooklinboatyard.com), phone cross-checked against its Google Maps listing; coordinates from Brooklin Boat Yard's verified map location.

properties.title: Naskeag Harbor — Anchorage

anchorage.anchoringNotes: A small, working harbor at Naskeag Point on the Jericho Bay side of Brooklin, heavily used by commercial lobster boats, with a granite-gravel town launch/landing at its edge. Neither the CCA Digital Cruising Guide nor Waterway Guide carries a dedicated anchorage entry for Naskeag Harbor (confirmed via direct site search) — treat this as a working harbor with no documented depths, holding, or mooring-rental service, rather than an established cruiser destination.
anchorage.notes: Public boat launch at Naskeag Point. Not to be confused with Atlantic Boat Company, whose yard is a few miles north on Flye Point/Herrick Bay, not in Naskeag Harbor itself.

properties.source: Coordinates from a Google Maps place marker for 'Naskeag Harbor' — approximate; no numeric position is given in any cruising-guide source found. Harbor-use description from Paddling.com (paddling.com/paddle/locations/naskeag-harbor-brooklin-maine) and US Harbors (usharbors.com/2012/05/exploring-brooklins-finest-in-springtime-naskeag-point/).

properties.title: Herrick Bay — Anchorage & Moorings

anchorage.moorings: Atlantic Boat Company (355 Flye Point Rd, Brooklin) rents seasonal and transient moorings on a first-come, first-served basis with a reservation form; call ahead to confirm availability. Renters get dinghy-float access and a hot shower/washer/dryer at the dockhouse. The yard also does haul-out and repair work.
anchorage.anchoringNotes: Good open-bay anchorage; holding is excellent in hard sand at 7–11 ft depth.
anchorage.holdingGround: Excellent holding in hard sand.
anchorage.protection: Exposed to wind and wake from the southeast; otherwise a broad, fairly open bay.
anchorage.contact: Atlantic Boat Company: (207) 359-4658, info@atlanticboat.com, VHF ch 10 (monitored weekdays 7am–3:30pm).

properties.source: Marinas.com Herrick Bay Anchorage listing (marinas.com/view/anchorage/6vf42m_Herrick_Bay_Anchorage_Brooklin_ME_United_States) for coordinates/depth/holding; Atlantic Boat Company (atlanticboat.com/moorings) for mooring/contact details, phone cross-checked against its Google Maps listing.

properties.title: Blue Hill Harbor — Anchorage & Moorings
properties.place: Blue Hill Harbor, Blue Hill, ME

anchorage.moorings: Kollegewidgwok Yacht Club (KYC) assigns moorings to visitors — hail 'KYC dock' on VHF ch 9 or call (207) 374-5581; moorings for boats over 50 ft are limited. KYC now takes phone reservations, but only within a day or so of arrival (previous policy was strictly first-come, first-served).
anchorage.anchoringNotes: Main anchorage is in the outer harbor, 23–50 ft; a second, more secluded anchorage lies farther in, past can #7 and nun #2, off the golf course, in 10–28 ft over soft bottom. Enter leaving cans #1 and #3 to port, then can #5 to port and nun #2 to starboard, rounding Sculpin Point (can submerge at high tide); a 'fisherman's channel' shortcut between Seal Rock and the Sculpin Point flagpole is only for shoal-draft or locally-experienced boats. Navigate by NOAA Chart 13316.
anchorage.holdingGround: Soft bottom in the inner, more secluded anchorage.
anchorage.protection: A wide, deep, well-protected bay; predictable afternoon sea breezes can kick up some chop, but the harbor itself is 'quite large and safe.'
anchorage.fee: $55 per night for a KYC mooring.
anchorage.contact: Kollegewidgwok Yacht Club: VHF ch 9, (207) 374-5581, kycbluehill.com. Blue Hill Town Office (mooring/outhaul permits): (207) 374-2281.
anchorage.notes: Blue Hill Town Wharf dries out at mean low water — time dinghy trips within a couple of hours of high tide or risk getting stuck on the flats; the town wharf is about a half-mile from the anchorage. Ethanol-free gas/diesel and water at the KYC dock; outside/intermittent pump-out; no shore power. The Town of Blue Hill separately manages a 600+ mooring/outhaul field under its own harbor ordinance and also maintains two complimentary moorings at an anchorage in South Blue Hill, about five miles away.

properties.source: Cruising Club of America Digital Cruising Guide to Maine, Blue Hill entry (guides.cruisingclub.org/harbor/blue-hill/), read in full; Town of Blue Hill mooring page (bluehillme.gov/town-services/moorings/); coordinates from Kollegewidgwok Yacht Club's verified Google Maps location, which anchors the main mooring field/anchorage.

properties.title: Hall Quarry
properties.place: West shore of Somes Sound, Mount Desert, Maine — about 1.7 NM north of Valley Cove

anchorage.moorings: Rental moorings (14 seasonal) via John M. Williams & Co. Boatyard, available July and August only; a ~20-ft alongside float for taking on water.
anchorage.anchoringNotes: Too deep for anchoring, per the CCA Cruising Guide.
anchorage.protection: Protected deep-water location, per the boatyard's own description.
anchorage.contact: John M. Williams & Co. Boatyard, 17 Shipwright Lane, Mount Desert, ME 04660, (207) 244-7854, https://www.jwboatco.com/
anchorage.notes: Site of a historic, now-inactive granite quarry on Somes Sound's west shore. The boatyard has a 50-ton Travelift and offers full-service repair/restoration (woodworking, fiberglass, metal, composite, paint, varnish) plus mechanical, electrical, engine, and plumbing work for power and sailboats up to 55 ft length / 7 ft draft, accommodating up to 200 boats; heated and unheated winter storage.

properties.source: CCA Cruising Guide to Maine, Somes Sound (https://guides.cruisingclub.org/harbor/somes-sound/); https://www.jwboatco.com/; coordinates via OpenStreetMap/Nominatim geocoding of 17 Shipwright Lane, Mount Desert, ME

properties.title: Henry R. Abel & Co. Yacht Yard / Abel's Lobster
properties.place: Eastern shore of Somes Sound near the head, Mount Desert, Maine, north of Hall Quarry

anchorage.moorings: Summer rental moorings and slips for lease via Dockwa.
anchorage.anchoringNotes: Plenty of room for anchoring in good-holding mud off Abel's, at the head of the sound.
anchorage.holdingGround: Good-holding mud
anchorage.contact: Henry R. Abel & Co. Yacht Yard, 20 Abel's Lane, Mount Desert, ME 04660, (207) 276-5057, https://www.abelyachtyard.com/, moorings/slips via Dockwa (dockwa.com/explore/destination/n8c5me-henry-r-abel-co-yacht-yard).
